title: Concurrency, Races and Locks
summary: Why tasks that share data produce timing-dependent bugs, and how atomic operations, locks and careful ordering prevent races and deadlocks, including in single-threaded JavaScript.

questions.prompt: What is a **race condition**? And what's the difference between **concurrency** and **parallelism**?
questions.hint: Think of the two ATMs, and of one waiter vs ten waiters.
keyPoints: A race condition is when the result depends on the timing/interleaving of operations on shared state
Typical shape is read-modify-write or check-then-act with a gap another task can slip into
Concurrency: multiple tasks in progress over overlapping time, possibly taking turns on one core
Parallelism: multiple tasks executing at the same instant on different cores
You can have concurrency without parallelism (e.g. JavaScript's event loop)

questions.hint: Node is single-threaded, but what happens at each `await`? And there may be several server processes.
keyPoints: It's a check-then-act race: two requests can both run the SELECT before either INSERTs
At each await other requests run, and multiple server processes run in parallel anyway
An in-memory lock in one Node process doesn't help across processes or machines
Fix: a UNIQUE constraint on users.name and handle the duplicate-key error as 409
Alternatively INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING and check rows affected; the database makes it atomic

questions.prompt: Name the **four conditions** required for deadlock. A money-transfer function does `lock(from); lock(to); move money; unlock both`. Show how it can deadlock and give a simple fix.
questions.hint: What if Alice sends to Bob at the same time Bob sends to Alice?
keyPoints: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait (the Coffman conditions)
transfer(A→B) locks A then waits for B while transfer(B→A) locks B then waits for A: a cycle
Fix: always acquire locks in a global order (e.g. lower account ID first), breaking circular wait
Other options: lock acquisition timeouts with retry, or acquiring both locks atomically
Databases detect such cycles and abort one transaction, so the app must retry

questions.prompt: (a) Two threads each run 4 atomic steps. How many possible interleavings are there? (b) A service holds one global lock for 200 µs on every request. What is its maximum throughput, and does adding cores help?
questions.hint: (a) Choose which slots belong to thread 1. (b) Only one request can be in the critical section at a time.
keyPoints: (a) C(8, 4) = 8! / (4! × 4!) = 70 interleavings
Shows why testing can't easily cover all schedules: it explodes combinatorially
(b) Max throughput = 1 / 200 µs = 5,000 requests per second
Adding cores doesn't raise that cap because the critical section is serial
Fix: shrink the critical section or use finer-grained locks (e.g. per key) so unrelated requests don't contend
questions.answer: (a) `C(8,4) = 70`. (b) `1 / 0.0002 s = 5,000 req/s`, regardless of core count; shorten or split the lock.

questions.prompt: An e-commerce site sells 100 units of a limited sneaker. During the drop, 30,000 requests per second hit the 'buy' button across 50 app servers, and after the sale the inventory shows `-37`. Why, and how would you make overselling impossible?
questions.hint: Where does the read-check-write happen, and where would a lock need to live to be seen by all 50 servers?
keyPoints: Read stock, check > 0, then write stock - 1 is a read-modify-write race across many concurrent requests
Locks inside each app server don't coordinate across 50 servers
Make the decrement atomic in the shared store: UPDATE items SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = ? AND stock > 0, and check rows affected
Alternatives: row lock in a transaction (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), optimistic version check, or an atomic DECR in Redis followed by a durable order record
Mentions the hot row becomes a bottleneck at high load, so consider a queue or pre-reserving tokens

questions.hint: Keep a count of free slots and a queue of waiting resolvers. `acquire()` returns a promise that resolves to a release function.
keyPoints: Tracks available permits and a FIFO queue of waiters
acquire() resolves immediately if a permit is free (decrementing it), otherwise enqueues a resolver
release() hands the permit to the next waiter if one exists, otherwise increments the count
Release is safe to call once (guards against double release) and is called in finally
Explains why this needs no atomic instructions in JS: the event loop runs each callback to completion
